title: The 1 kHz Filter That Only Passed 70.7%
featured_title: THE 1 KHZ FILTER THAT ONLY PASSED 70.7%
subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students

presentation.challenge: A 'passband' tone reached the cutoff and lost nearly 30% of its amplitude.

practice.primary_question: Why is a first-order low-pass already attenuated to 70.7% at its cutoff frequency?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Treating cutoff as a brick-wall passband boundary with unity gain.

case_dna.target_misconception: A low-pass filter passes the cutoff frequency with essentially no attenuation because cutoff marks the end of the passband.
case_dna.why_plausible: Cutoff is often described casually as the passband edge, hiding the precise first-order definition of -3 dB or 1/sqrt(2) magnitude.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: For a first-order RC low-pass at f = fc, |H| = 1/sqrt(2) = 0.707, so a 2.00 V peak sinusoid becomes about 1.414 V peak.
case_dna.corrected_model: Treat cutoff as the -3 dB point, not a zero-loss boundary. Use |H| = 1/sqrt(1+(f/fc)^2) and choose fc from the allowed amplitude loss.

problem_statement: A first-order RC low-pass is specified with fc = 1.0 kHz. A 1.0 kHz, 2.00 V peak sensor tone is expected to pass almost unchanged, but the measured output is about 1.41 V peak. Diagnose the missing amplitude and choose a higher cutoff that keeps at least 90% of the 1 kHz amplitude.
fixed_constraints: At least 90% amplitude is required at 1.0 kHz

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The signal is at cutoff, but nearly 30% of its amplitude is gone.
gates.prompt: What does cutoff frequency actually mean for a first-order low-pass?

options.label: At cutoff, magnitude is 1/sqrt(2), about 0.707 of input
options.reason: The first-order cutoff is the -3 dB point.

options.label: At cutoff, gain is exactly 1 and attenuation begins only above it
options.reason: Cutoff is not a brick-wall boundary; magnitude is already 0.707 at fc.

options.label: At cutoff, amplitude is exactly one-half
options.reason: Half power corresponds to about 0.707 amplitude, not 0.5 amplitude.

options.label: A 1.41 V reading proves the capacitor is faulty
options.reason: 1.41 V is the expected ideal response from a 2.00 V input at fc.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the output at cutoff
gates.prompt: If Vin = 2.00 V peak and |H(fc)| = 0.707, what output amplitude (V peak) do you expect?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Drive the filter at 1 kHz
gates.result: The 2.00 V peak input produces about 1.414 V peak at the 1.0 kHz cutoff.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the cutoff amplitude
gates.prompt: Calculate 2.00/sqrt(2). Enter the output in V peak.
gates.success: Vout = 2.00/sqrt(2) ≈ 1.414 V peak, the first-order -3 dB cutoff response.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The response curve explains the loss

cards.text: 0.707 amplitude is the standard -3 dB cutoff point.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the filter review
report: C1. The filter is first-order low-pass with fc = 1.0 kHz.
C2. The input is a 1.0 kHz sinusoid at 2.00 V peak.
C3. Because the signal is still in the passband, the output should remain essentially 2.00 V peak at cutoff.

claims.label: C1
claims.reason: C1 is the stated filter condition.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: C2 is the stated test signal.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: C3 treats cutoff as an ideal brick-wall boundary; a first-order filter is already at 0.707 at fc.

evidence_choices.label: At fc, |H| = 0.707 and 2.00 V becomes 1.414 V
evidence_choices.reason: This directly matches the measurement and first-order filter law.

evidence_choices.label: The capacitor is connected to ground
evidence_choices.reason: Topology alone does not give the cutoff magnitude.

evidence_choices.label: The input frequency is exactly 1 kHz
evidence_choices.reason: Frequency equality matters only with the magnitude-response relation.

correction.template: At cutoff the gain is {gain}, so a 2.00 V peak input produces about {output} V peak.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Keep at least 90% of the 1 kHz amplitude
gates.constraint: At 1.0 kHz, |H| must be at least 0.90 for a first-order low-pass.

options.label: Raise the cutoff to about 2.2 kHz
options.reason: At fc = 2.2 kHz, |H| ≈ 0.91, meeting the 90% requirement.

options.label: Set fc to 707 Hz because 0.707 is the desired gain
options.reason: 0.707 is the gain at cutoff, not a frequency rule.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the cutoff rule
gates.prompt: A first-order low-pass has fc = 2 kHz and is driven at 2 kHz. What is its magnitude ratio?

options.reason: At its own cutoff a first-order low-pass has magnitude 1/sqrt(2).
Unity gain is the low-frequency limit.
Cutoff is half power, corresponding to 0.707 amplitude.
A first-order low-pass does not drop to zero at cutoff.

gates.explanation: At f = fc, the ideal first-order low-pass magnitude is always 0.707.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the analog-filter analysis
gates.confirmation: I confirm that a first-order cutoff frequency is the -3 dB point and not a zero-attenuation passband boundary.

items.label: What was measured
items.value: A 2.00 V peak input became about 1.414 V peak at 1 kHz.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: The cutoff frequency is already the -3 dB point.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use the magnitude response to place fc according to allowed attenuation.

seo.seo_title: RC Low-Pass Cutoff: Why Gain Is 0.707 at fc | FE E-024
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-024: a 1 kHz RC low-pass turns 2.00 V into 1.41 V at cutoff. Learn the -3 dB rule and choose a better cutoff.
seo.focus_keyphrase: RC low pass cutoff FE exam
seo.excerpt: Cutoff does not mean fully passed. A first-order low-pass is already at 0.707 amplitude at fc.
seo.direct_answer: For a first-order RC low-pass, the cutoff frequency is the -3 dB point. At f = fc, |H| = 1/sqrt(2) ≈ 0.707, so a 2.00 V peak input becomes about 1.414 V peak.

faqs.q: What is the gain of a first-order low-pass at cutoff?
Why is cutoff called the half-power point?
faqs.a: Because power is proportional to amplitude squared, so 0.707² is about 0.5.

faqs.q: How do I reduce attenuation at a frequency of interest?
faqs.a: Place the cutoff sufficiently above that frequency based on the allowed magnitude loss.
